decisions.title: Normalized Lifecycle Event Envelope
decisions.description: Hooks receive normalized event objects with a stable shape: event name, tool name, input, result, error, and duration. This means every hook can parse and react to events using the same interface, regardless of which tool triggered the event. The envelope makes hooks composable and testable.
decisions.alternatives: Passing raw tool call data to hooks is simpler but couples hooks to tool implementation details. A string-based event system loses structure and makes parsing fragile.

decisions.title: Hooks Observe, Block, or Annotate -- Never Replace
decisions.description: Hooks are constrained to three actions: observe (read-only side effects like logging), block (prevent execution and return a denial), or annotate (add metadata to the result). Hooks cannot replace the tool's return value or modify the conversation state directly. This keeps the main loop's state machine clean and prevents hooks from secretly becoming a second control plane.
decisions.alternatives: Allowing hooks to modify results freely creates a tangled mess where the tool says one thing but the hook changes it. Allowing hooks to inject messages into the conversation breaks the loop's message-ordering guarantees.

decisions.title: Named Registration Points, Not Arbitrary Injection
decisions.description: Hooks register at named lifecycle points (pre_tool, post_tool, on_error, on_start, on_end) rather than injecting at arbitrary positions in the loop. Named points keep the hook surface stable and predictable. New hooks can be added without understanding the entire loop internals -- just pick a named point and register.
decisions.alternatives: Middleware-style wrapping (each hook wraps the next) is powerful but creates invisible chains that are hard to debug. Event bus patterns (pub/sub on arbitrary topics) are flexible but lose the predictable ordering that named registration points provide.
